stances.claim: Lucila Takjerad's Harvard commencement insight -- that 'the least you can do might turn out to be the most significant' -- reframes ambition itself: alongside doing one's noble most, one must do the obscure least, because small gestures (like writing an illiterate mother's name on a list) can unlock entire life trajectories.
stances.rhetorical_move: borrowed-commencement framing (using another's speech as the thematic anchor)

stances.claim: CJ's own life confirms Takjerad's principle: he peddled newspapers, shined shoes, sold bibles and textbooks; was orphaned during law school; was hospitalized during the first Sunday of bar exams; and nearly quit -- but Salonga's mentorship and an old friend's small gesture of paying for his bar review (on condition of a Top Ten finish) ushered him to the noble legal profession and ultimately the highest judicial post.
stances.rhetorical_move: autobiographical-confirmation arc (CJ's life as proof of Takjerad's principle)

stances.claim: The FLP's gifts to scholars -- financial grants, Supreme Court interviews, tough judges' questions, midnight dissertation labors, secretariat kindnesses -- are themselves 'valuable little things' that may have twisted and turned their careers as much as their formal achievements.
stances.rhetorical_move: institutional-gifts-as-little-things (extending the metaphor to the FLP itself)

stances.claim: DiGi Age robots will not eliminate lawyers -- contrary to predictions -- because lawyers bred in liberty and prosperity have the heart and wisdom to dispense compassionate, empathetic justice especially when the law is inadequate, unclear, or unconscionable, which robots cannot.
stances.rhetorical_move: AI-skepticism with virtue-anchored counter-argument (legal compassion as the irreducible human element)

stances.claim: Within ten or twenty years the FLP scholars will be DiGi Age leaders, and even if CJ is no longer around, his spirit 'will be hovering above you, behind you, and beside you, smiling and contented' -- that he brought them little things that twisted their careers toward building a just and humane society under the rule of law in the DiGi Age.
stances.rhetorical_move: legacy-pledge closing (rare CJ moment of explicit valediction)

notable_anecdotes: Lucila Takjerad's mother's emigration story -- 1994 Algerian civil war, walking the public market, learning of the France emigration list, being illiterate and unable to write her name, walking away dejected, then being chased by a man who wrote it for her -- the central parable of the column and the original instance of 'the least you can do.'

CJ's autobiographical reveal: peddling newspapers, shining shoes, selling bibles and textbooks; his father (high school graduate, lowly government employee) dying during his pre-law years; his unemployed mother (elementary graduate) dying in his senior year of law; the bar-exam hospitalization on the first Sunday -- the most concentrated single-paragraph autobiographical capsule in CJ's columns.

Dr. Jovito R. Salonga as FEU law dean refusing to let CJ quit the bar exams -- a sentence that links this column to the closing tribute in C17 ('the 100th birthday of the late Dr. Jovito R. Salonga, my esteemed guru'), making C17 and D21 a pair on Salonga.

The unnamed old friend (now deceased) who paid for CJ's bar review on condition of Top Ten finish -- a story CJ rarely tells, deployed here as the personal exemplar of Takjerad's 'least you can do' principle.
CJ's sixth-place bar finish 'with God's grace' -- a rare CJ humility-marker tying personal achievement to providence.
The closing 'my spirit will be hovering above you, behind you, and beside you, smiling and contented' -- one of CJ's most explicit valedictory passages in his column corpus.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban summarizes his commencement-style address at the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity (FLP) awarding ceremonies -- honoring bar topnotchers, scholars, valedictorians, and dissertation-writing contest winners -- held via Zoom on June 12, 2020. He builds the address around Lucila Takjerad's Harvard commencement story from a year earlier: in 1994, during the Algerian civil war, Lucila's poor illiterate mother walked through a public market, learned a France emigration list was open, but could not write her own name; an unnamed man chased her and wrote it for her, transporting the family to France where Lucila grew up to graduate from Harvard. Lucila's message -- 'of course, do the most you can do... But also, do the least you can do. Because, the least you can do might turn out to be the most significant' -- leads CJ to his own autobiographical confirmation: peddling newspapers, shining shoes, selling bibles and textbooks; orphaned during law school (his father, a high school graduate and lowly government employee, dying during his pre-law years and his unemployed mother in his senior year); hospitalized on the first Sunday of his bar exams; ready to quit until his FEU law dean Dr. Jovito R. Salonga refused to let him, and until an old friend (now deceased) paid for his bar review on condition of a Top Ten finish -- leading to his sixth-place finish 'with God's grace' and ultimately the highest judicial post. He extends the metaphor to the FLP's own gifts -- financial grants, Supreme Court interviews, judges' tough questions, midnight dissertations, secretariat kindness -- as 'valuable little things' that may twist and turn careers more decisively than the formal honors. He closes with an AI-age credo: contrary to predictions, DiGi Age robots will not eliminate lawyers, because 'lawyers bred in liberty and prosperity... have the heart and the wisdom to dispense compassionate justice especially when the law is inadequate, unclear, or unconscionable.' And with one of his most explicit valedictory passages: in ten or twenty years, when the scholars are DiGi Age leaders, 'my spirit will be hovering above you, behind you, and beside you, smiling and contented, that I have brought you a few little things that made a vital difference in twisting and turning your lives and careers to build a just and humane society under the rule of law in the DiGi Age.'
